questions.q: What is the difference between Platform Cache's session cache and org cache scopes?
options: Session cache is tied to one user's current session; org cache is shared across every user and session in the org
Session cache is permanent, while org cache automatically expires after one hour
Org cache can only store numbers, while session cache can store any data type
They are two names for exactly the same scope with no actual difference
questions.explain: Session cache is per-user and per-session, suited to data relevant only to that one interaction; org cache is shared org-wide, suited to data that's the same for every user, like a computed configuration lookup.

questions.q: Why is checking contains() before reading a value from Platform Cache not optional?
options: Because contains() is required by Apex syntax and the code won't compile without it
Because Platform Cache automatically deletes all data every 24 hours regardless of settings
Because Platform Cache uses LRU eviction and explicit time-to-live, so a previously-cached value is not guaranteed to still be present, and skipping the check risks a null reference error
Because contains() is what actually stores the value in the cache
questions.explain: LRU eviction and time-to-live mean a cached value can disappear between one read and the next, so code must handle a cache miss gracefully rather than assuming the cached value is always there.

questions.q: What kind of data is the strongest candidate for Platform Cache, according to this lesson?
options: Data that changes on every single transaction and is unique to each record
Data that is cheap to query and rarely ever read
Any data at all — caching has no meaningful tradeoffs to consider
Data that is expensive to compute or query, shared or reused across many transactions, and doesn't change often
questions.explain: Caching earns its cost specifically on data that's expensive to produce but reused often without changing — frequently-read, rarely-changed configuration data is the textbook example.

questions.q: Why is caching the wrong fix for a query that is slow because it's genuinely non-selective (per Lesson 4)?
options: Because Platform Cache cannot be used with any SOQL query results under any circumstances
Because caching just delays when the expensive query cost is paid rather than reducing it — the underlying selectivity problem still needs to be fixed directly
Because non-selective queries are actually faster than caching in every case
Because caching automatically rewrites a query to be more selective
questions.explain: Caching is a complement to an already-efficient query that's just being run more often than necessary — it doesn't fix an inherently expensive, non-selective query, which still needs the Lesson 4 fix applied directly.

questions.q: In the Apex org cache example, what does passing 3600 to orgPart.put() represent?
options: The time-to-live in seconds for how long that cached value should be kept before it needs to be refreshed
The maximum number of records the cached value can contain
The governor limit cost, in CPU milliseconds, of storing the value
The maximum heap size, in bytes, allocated to the cache partition
questions.explain: The third argument to Cache.OrgPartition.put() sets the time-to-live (in seconds) for that cached value, after which it's expected to be refreshed rather than trusted as current.
